final_answer:
A good way to see the process is: it is a bounded-depth Goodstein process with an extra finite “countdown” coordinate. The countdown decreases when \(k>0\), and when \(k=0\), the hereditary base-change-minus-one step decreases the associated ordinal.

Let
\[
\alpha(t)=o_b(t).
\]
First note that base change preserves ordinal interpretation:
\[
o_{b+1}(\mathrm{BC}_b(t))=o_b(t),
\]
because the ordinal interpretation replaces the base symbol by \(\omega\), so changing \(b\) to \(b+1\) does not change the formal ordinal.

Now we need the subtraction fact: if \(0\ne t\in\mathcal T_2(b)\), then
\[
o_{b+1}(G_b(t))<o_b(t).
\]
This is the usual hereditary-base borrow argument. Write
\[
t=c_1b^{e_1}+\cdots+c_mb^{e_m},
\qquad
\nu_b(e_1)>\cdots>\nu_b(e_m)\ge0.
\]
After base change, subtracting \(1\) either reduces a nonzero constant coefficient, or, if the last exponent is positive, borrows from the final term. The borrowed part expands into powers with exponents numerically below \(\nu_{b+1}(\mathrm{BC}_b(e_m))\). Numerical order of canonical bounded-depth terms agrees with their ordinal order, so all those new exponents have ordinal interpretation strictly below \(o_b(e_m)\). Thus the Cantor normal form ordinal strictly decreases.

Therefore every nonterminal step decreases
\[
\rho_b(t,k)=\omega^{o_b(t)}(k+1).
\]
Indeed, if \(k>0\), then
\[
\rho_{b+1}(\mathrm{BC}_b(t),k-1)
=\omega^{o_b(t)}k
<
\omega^{o_b(t)}(k+1).
\]
If \(k=0\) and \(t\ne0\), then
\[
o_{b+1}(G_b(t))<o_b(t),
\]
so
\[
\rho_{b+1}(G_b(t),b)
=
\omega^{o_{b+1}(G_b(t))}(b+1)
<
\omega^{o_b(t)}
=
\rho_b(t,0).
\]
There is no infinite strictly decreasing sequence of ordinals, so every nested run terminates.

For \(\Theta\), at fixed base \(b\), depth \(1\) exponents have ordinal supremum \(\omega^b\), hence depth \(2\) terms have ordinal supremum
\[
\omega^{\omega^b}.
\]
Taking the supremum over all finite \(b\ge2\),
\[
\sup_{b,t} o_b(t)
=
\sup_{b\ge2}\omega^{\omega^b}
=
\omega^{\omega^\omega}.
\]
Thus
\[
\Theta
=
\sup \bigl(\omega^{o_b(t)}(k+1)+1\bigr)
=
\omega^{\omega^{\omega^\omega}}.
\]

Now compute \(o_3(t_\star)\). We have
\[
e_1=2\cdot3^2+3+2,
\qquad
e_2=3^2+2,
\qquad
e_3=2\cdot3+1,
\]
so
\[
o_{3,1}(e_1)=\omega^2\cdot2+\omega+2,
\]
\[
o_{3,1}(e_2)=\omega^2+2,
\]
\[
o_{3,1}(e_3)=\omega\cdot2+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
o_3(t_\star)
=
\omega^{\omega^2\cdot2+\omega+2}\cdot2
+\omega^{\omega^2+2}
+\omega^{\omega\cdot2+1}\cdot2
+1.
\]
Since \(k=2\),
\[
\rho_3(t_\star,2)
=
\omega^{o_3(t_\star)}\cdot3.
\]

Hence the requested exact pair is
\[
\boxed{
\left(
\omega^{\omega^{\omega^\omega}},
\;
\omega^{
\omega^{\omega^2\cdot2+\omega+2}\cdot2
+\omega^{\omega^2+2}
+\omega^{\omega\cdot2+1}\cdot2
+1
}\cdot3
\right)
}.
\]
